analysis.one_liner: Criminalizes and claws back private equity pay when health care acquisitions fail and patients are harmed.
analysis.headline: A bill to claw back up to 10 years of pay from private equity executives when their health care takeovers fail and patients are hurt has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since its February 2026 introduction, with five Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a crime, punishable by one to six years in prison, for private equity executives and owners whose actions contribute to a health care company they took over missing payroll, missing rent, defaulting on loans, closing, or going bankrupt. It would let the Justice Department and state attorneys general claw back up to 10 years of the executives' compensation — dividends, management fees, sale proceeds, golden parachutes — and use the money to cover unpaid worker wages and pensions and community health needs. It would also end special tax breaks for real estate investment trusts that buy up hospital property, cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to REITs, require large health care entities to publicly report their ownership and finances, and order a federal study of profit-driven practices in care delivery.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, and doctor practices owned by private equity, who have faced closures, staff cuts, and unpaid bills after leveraged buyouts. Health care workers, because clawed-back money goes first to cover their unpaid salaries, benefits, and pensions. Taxpayers, who currently subsidize health care REITs through the tax code.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime, with 1 to 6 years imprisonment, for covered parties at private equity firms whose actions contribute to a triggering event — missed payroll for over a quarter of the workforce, closure, missed rent, loan default, or bankruptcy — that kills or injures patients at the acquired firm. [S2]

Allows the Attorney General or state attorneys general to claw back all or part of 10 years of compensation — including dividends, management and monitoring fees, profits from asset sales, and golden parachutes — and directs the money to unpaid employee salaries and benefits, pension shortfalls in bankruptcy, and the health needs of the harmed community. [S2]

Ends the special tax treatment of 'qualified health care property' held by real estate investment trusts and eliminates the deduction for qualified REIT dividends, closing tax advantages that reward sale-leaseback deals in health care. [S2]
Bars Medicare and Medicaid participation for any provider that sells assets to, or pledges assets as loan collateral with, a health care REIT after enactment. [S2]

Requires hospitals, health systems, private-equity-owned practices, hospices, dialysis facilities and other covered entities to report annually on ownership, debt, lease payments to landlords, investor fees and dividends, and foreign domiciles, posted on a public HHS website, with fines up to $5 million per false or missing report. [S2]

Orders the HHS Inspector General to study profit-driven practices — upcoding, staffing cuts, insurer denial tactics, and evasion of state corporate-practice-of-medicine laws — and their impact on patient care and public health programs. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Private equity executives, general partners, and private funds that own health care companies, who face prison time, civil penalties of up to five times any clawback, and loss of compensation going back 10 years. Health care REITs and their investors, who lose a dedicated tax rule and their pipeline of new health care landlord deals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The criminal provision applies when a covered party's actions merely 'contributed' to a triggering event, and triggering events include ordinary financial distress such as missing rent or defaulting on a loan for 90 days — a scope that could chill legitimate capital investment in struggling health care facilities. [S2]

Cutting off Medicare and Medicaid for any provider that sells property to a REIT is a blunt tool: a facility that needs to sell real estate to stay afloat would instead lose its main revenue stream, potentially forcing closure and disrupting patients' care. [S2]
The clawback and liability regime applies only to health care corporations acquired in change-of-control transactions, leaving harm from other corporate ownership structures untouched. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a documented pattern — private equity extracting dividends, fees, and sale-leaseback profits from health care firms that later miss payroll or collapse — and its worker-and-patient-first clawback fund is a genuine remedy. The criminal penalty's breadth and the all-or-nothing Medicare/Medicaid exclusion for REIT deals are real design risks that could push distressed facilities toward closure rather than rescue. On balance the public benefits outweigh the costs, but the enforcement provisions are broad enough that a careful drafter would narrow them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day in February 2026, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — has been taken since.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Corporate Crimes Against Health Care Act on February 11, 2026, joined by four Democratic cosponsors: Senators Blumenthal, Markey, Merkley, and Welch. [S1]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and the action history shows no activity since that referral. [S4]

The Finance Committee, which holds jurisdiction over both the criminal clawback provisions' tax-adjacent health program exclusions and the bill's tax title, has taken no steps toward a hearing or markup in the record. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity firms and health care real estate investment trusts are better off so far: the bill has not moved in committee, so the clawback, criminal penalties, REIT tax repeal, and ownership disclosure requirements they would face have not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and health care REITs

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled four Senate cosponsors for it.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Markey, Merkley, and Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only recorded supporters.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Republicans in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in February 2026 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats and no Republican cosponsor has joined; the bill now sits with the Republican-led Senate Finance Committee, which has not acted on it.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and their executives
industries.note: The bill exposes executives, control persons, and private funds to prison terms and clawback of up to 10 years of compensation — dividends, management and monitoring fees, asset-sale profits, golden parachutes — whenever an acquired health care firm misses payroll, closes, defaults, or goes bankrupt. The industry profits by extracting these payments from leveraged health care companies, so its interest runs directly against the patients and workers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: The bill repeals the special tax rule for health care property held by REITs, eliminates the deduction for REIT dividends, and cuts off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to REITs. REITs make money leasing hospitals and nursing homes their own real estate back at rising rents, a cost that lands on patients and public programs.

industries.industry: Corporate owners of hospitals, physician practices, and other providers
industries.note: Covered entities must disclose ownership chains, debt, landlord payments, investor fees, and foreign domiciles on a public website, with fines up to $5 million per false or missing report. Their current ability to keep these arrangements opaque is what the transparency requirement removes.

industries.industry: Health care workers and their pension funds
industries.note: Clawed-back compensation is directed first to unpaid salaries and benefits, and in bankruptcy to pension fund shortfalls. Workers are beneficiaries rather than an industry the bill regulates; the bill explicitly exempts pension funds from liability.

analysis.trajectory: With no action in the 11 months since referral, no Republican support, and a Republican-run Finance Committee, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup this Congress. Its most realistic path is being folded in part — such as the ownership disclosure provisions — into a larger health or tax package, or reintroduction in a future Congress.
